title: Sherlock Holmes: The Man, The Myth
summary: Josh and Chuck (with iHeart Intro voice) discuss Sherlock Holmes, the fictional consulting detective created by Arthur Conan Doyle. Topics include Holmes's character traits and deductive reasoning, Watson as sidekick, the story formula and the Strand Magazine serialization, illustrator Sidney Paget and the deerstalker and calabash pipe imagery, Doyle's life and spiritualism, real-life inspirations such as Joseph Bell and Jerome Caminada, forensic science influence, Baker Street Irregulars and the Grand Game, the many adaptations (Jeremy Brett, Benedict Cumberbatch, Guy Ritchie, Elementary, Billy Wilder's Private Life of Sherlock Holmes, The Seven-Per-Cent Solution), and the copyright history of the Conan Doyle Estate, which ended with the stories entering the public domain. The episode closes with a listener email about Trinidad and the anaconda episode.

entities.name: The Private Life of Sherlock Holmes

segments.title: Opening banter on Sherlock Holmes movies and reading
segments.summary: The hosts chat about whether listeners have read Sherlock Holmes stories and seen the movies, including The House of Fear and the Will Ferrell and John C. Reilly version.

segments.title: Holmes as consulting detective and his popularity
segments.summary: Holmes is described as the world's first consulting detective, distinct from Scotland Yard. He is the most frequently portrayed human literary character on screen, and the hosts discuss how deductive reasoning separates him from other mysteries.

segments.title: Holmes's personality, habits and Irene Adler
segments.summary: The hosts describe Holmes as a genius who is flawed, arrogant and emotionally distant, with allusions to cocaine use, boxing, violin and a brother. They discuss Irene Adler and Moriarty as foils.

segments.title: Publication history: A Study in Scarlet and The Strand
segments.summary: A Study in Scarlet first appeared in Beeton's Christmas Annual in 1887. The shorter stories in The Strand Magazine made the character popular with a newly literate British readership.

segments.title: Story formula and short story appeal
segments.summary: The hosts describe the repeated formula of the stories, with a client visit at 221B Baker Street, deductions, investigation, and a Watson-narrated explanation. Short length appealed to younger readers.

segments.title: Sidney Paget's illustrations and the deerstalker cap
segments.summary: Sidney Paget illustrated the stories and modeled Holmes on his brother Walter, a claim the hosts say is disputed. The deerstalker cap and calabash pipe became iconic, though Doyle described only a close-fitting cloth cap.

segments.title: Watson's background and Holmes's scientific methods
segments.summary: Watson is introduced as a wounded army medic from Afghanistan and the heart of the partnership. Doyle's medical training and the cutting-edge forensic techniques of the era informed the stories, reflecting pre-World War One faith in science.

segments.title: Holmes's superpowers and selective knowledge
segments.summary: The hosts list Holmes's deductive abilities, such as identifying tobacco ash and tire treads, and discuss his deliberate ignorance of irrelevant facts like the Earth orbiting the Sun. They also note his drive to correct police failures such as the Jack the Ripper case.

segments.title: Holmes and Victorian social hierarchy
segments.summary: Holmes is described as an upholder of Victorian social order who also criticized its arbitrary class hierarchies without trying to change them.

segments.title: Arthur Conan Doyle's life and early career
segments.summary: Doyle was from Edinburgh, trained as a doctor, worked as a ship doctor, and sold his first story for a small fee. Ward Lock published A Study in Scarlet after a publisher's wife urged it. He was paid well for the Strand stories but considered himself a better writer of other fiction, such as The Lost World.

segments.title: Doyle's attempt to kill Holmes and spiritualism
segments.summary: Doyle tried to end Holmes's story and grew tired of him. The hosts also mention Doyle's later spiritualism after his son's death in 1918 and his belief in the Cottingham fairies photographs.

segments.title: Doyle's friendship with Houdini and real-life inspirations
segments.summary: Doyle and Houdini were an odd pair, since Houdini was a skeptic of mediums. The hosts discuss Joseph Bell as the primary model for Holmes's deductive style, and Jerome Caminada as another possible inspiration.

segments.title: Life imitating art: forensic practice and The Problem of Thor Bridge
segments.summary: Real investigators such as Edmund Locard and Hans Gross adopted methods from the Holmes stories. The Problem of Thor Bridge inspired real suicides staged as homicides, and Doyle may have drawn on an 1893 Hans Gross case.

segments.title: Holmes's popularity, fandom origins and resurrection
segments.summary: Doyle was surprised by the character's popularity. Fan fiction such as Jerome K. Jerome's parody is cited, and readers protested the death of Holmes, with many Strand subscribers cancelling. Doyle wrote The Hound of the Baskervilles as a prequel and revived Holmes in 1903.

segments.title: Sherlockian fandom and the Grand Game
segments.summary: The hosts explain Sherlockians and Holmesians who treat the stories as real history, a practice called the Grand Game. Ronald Knox's 1911 spoof gave rise to the idea of an official canon. The Baker Street Irregulars in New York, founded in 1934, is discussed.

segments.title: Local Sherlock Holmes societies
segments.summary: The hosts mention the Shaka Sherlockians of Hawaii, which the Baker Street Irregulars recognized with official status.

segments.title: Film and TV adaptations
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the many adaptations, including The Hound of the Baskervilles stage play with the line elementary my dear fellow, Billy Wilder's The Private Life of Sherlock Holmes, Jeremy Brett's Granada series, the Guy Ritchie films, Cumberbatch's Sherlock, Elementary with Johnny Lee Miller, and Enola Holmes.

segments.title: Recommended viewing and modern settings
segments.summary: The hosts suggest where to start with Holmes, including Elementary and Mr. Holmes with Ian McKellen. Elementary's Johnny Lee Miller played Holmes in 154 episodes, and modern adaptations are contrasted with the Victorian originals.

segments.title: Copyright and the Conan Doyle Estate
segments.summary: After Doyle died in 1930, his heirs formed Conan Doyle Estate Limited, which controlled Holmes rights and charged for use. The Seven Per Cent Solution was made after a dispute over rights. The copyright expired in the UK in 2000 and in the US in 1998, but the estate argued the stories should be treated as one work, and a judge rejected that argument.

segments.title: Estate licensing and future Holmes parodies
segments.summary: The hosts note that the estate authenticated new works to give them official status and speculate about future uses of the character, including a dark parody, which they agree would be a bad idea.

segments.title: Shoutouts and sign-off transition
segments.summary: The hosts thank writer Kyle and friend of the show Richard Fallwall, who recommended Stephen Fry's audiobook collection of the Holmes canon. They transition to the listener mail segment.

segments.title: Listener mail about Trinidad and the anaconda
segments.summary: A listener from Trinidad explains that the island is continental, once connected to Venezuela by a land bridge during the last Ice Age, which explains the shared fauna and anacondas. This answers the hosts' earlier question from the anaconda episode.

segments.title: Closing credits
segments.summary: Josh thanks the listener and gives the email address. The iHeart Intro closes with production credits.
